task_2.title: Update build metadata and setuptools minimum to remove packaging warnings
task_2.description: Version 2.11.0 updates the package build configuration to remove setuptools deprecation warnings around license metadata and raises the required setuptools version for builds to 77.0.3 or newer so the package can be built cleanly with current packaging standards.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure upgrading to 2.11.0 removes package build warnings caused by deprecated license metadata and requires a compatible setuptools version so builds succeed cleanly under current packaging standards.

expectation.grounded: Building the library with version 2.11.0 should no longer emit the documented setuptools deprecation warnings related to legacy license classifier usage or deprecated table-based `project.license` metadata. The package's build dependency contract should require `setuptools` version 77.0.3 or higher for build-time compatibility. No runtime API additions, removals, or behavior changes are evidenced by the provided code diff.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should modernize packaging metadata so consumers and maintainers can build the library without deprecation noise, while clearly requiring a new enough build toolchain to support that metadata format. Application behavior at runtime should remain unchanged.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime-facing behavior, public API changes, or altered exception semantics beyond the build-time dependency requirement. Preserve successful package builds while eliminating the specific packaging warnings described in the release note.
constraints.conceptual: The change should be limited to build and packaging compatibility. It should not change how the library behaves for normal application use.

behavior: Package builds target updated license metadata conventions that avoid setuptools deprecation warnings.
Build environments must satisfy a minimum `setuptools` version of 77.0.3.
The supplied evidence indicates a build-system and dependency update rather than a runtime library behavior change.
acceptance_criteria: When the library is built using a build environment with `setuptools` 77.0.3 or newer, it should build without the deprecated license metadata warnings described in the release note.
When an upgrader evaluates the 2.11.0 release, they should understand that the required build dependency floor for `setuptools` has increased to 77.0.3.
When the library is used at runtime after the upgrade, it should preserve existing application-facing behavior because no runtime change is evidenced by the provided release materials.

task_4.title: Make PyJWKSet directly iterable
task_4.description: Version 2.11.0 adds direct iteration support for JWK sets so callers can iterate over a PyJWKSet itself instead of reaching into its internal key collection. This improves the public API ergonomics while preserving existing key lookup behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWK sets can be consumed as standard iterables so application code can loop over their keys directly without depending on internal collection access.

expectation.grounded: PyJWKSet should expose iterator behavior through its public API so iterating a PyJWKSet yields the same contained PyJWK objects as its existing keys collection. This should support normal Python iteration consumers such as for-loops and list construction while keeping existing get_key lookup behavior intact.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to treat a JWK set like a normal collection of keys and iterate over it directly, with each iteration item being one key object from the set.

constraints.grounded: Iteration must yield PyJWK entries from the current set without changing lookup semantics for key IDs. Existing key retrieval by kid must continue to return the matching key and continue to raise KeyError when no matching key exists.
constraints.conceptual: The new iterable behavior should be additive only: it should make key sets easier to consume without changing how key lookup or missing-key failures behave.

behavior: PyJWKSet instances are directly iterable.
Iterating a PyJWKSet yields the same key objects contained in the set's existing key collection.
The iteration order follows the underlying stored key sequence.
Existing lookup of a key by kid remains available and continues to fail with KeyError when the requested key is absent.
acceptance_criteria: When application code iterates over a PyJWKSet, it should receive each PyJWK in the set without needing to access a separate keys attribute.
When a PyJWKSet is passed to standard iteration consumers such as a for-loop or list(), it should behave as an iterable of PyJWK objects.
When key IDs are looked up through the existing key retrieval API, matching keys should still be returned exactly as before.
When a requested key ID is not present in the set, the existing key retrieval API should still raise KeyError.

task_1.title: Enforce RFC-compliant ECDSA curve validation
task_1.description: The upgrade hardens ECDSA JWT handling so each standard ES algorithm only accepts elliptic-curve keys on its RFC-required curve. This prevents mismatched EC keys from being used for signing or verification and can cause previously accepted configurations to fail at runtime.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that ECDSA JWT operations reject elliptic-curve keys that do not match the selected ES algorithm's required curve, while continuing to accept correctly matched keys.

expectation.grounded: Default ECDSA algorithms returned by get_default_algorithms() must enforce curve matching for their registered algorithm names: ES256 with P-256/SECP256R1, ES256K with secp256k1/SECP256K1, ES384 with P-384/SECP384R1, and ES512 plus the ES521 compatibility alias with P-521/SECP521R1. ECAlgorithm.prepare_key() must validate the curve for direct EC key objects and for keys loaded from PEM or SSH public/private key material, and it must raise InvalidKeyError when the key is an EC key on the wrong curve. This validation must be observable through normal jwt.encode() and jwt.decode() flows because they rely on the same key preparation path.
expectation.conceptual: Using an ECDSA JWT algorithm with the wrong elliptic-curve key should fail immediately instead of producing or accepting a token. Correctly matched keys should continue to work for signing and verification.

constraints.grounded: Curve enforcement applies when an ECAlgorithm instance has an expected curve configured, and the default registered ES algorithms must be configured that way. Custom ECAlgorithm instances created without an expected curve must remain able to accept supported EC curves without curve-specific rejection. Existing acceptance of valid EC key encodings and existing non-EC key type validation must not regress.
constraints.conceptual: The change should tighten security for standard ES algorithms without breaking valid same-curve usage or removing intentionally unrestricted ECAlgorithm behavior for advanced callers.

behavior: ES256 must reject EC keys not on P-256/SECP256R1 during key preparation, signing, and verification by raising InvalidKeyError.
ES256K must reject EC keys not on secp256k1/SECP256K1 by raising InvalidKeyError.
ES384 must reject EC keys not on P-384/SECP384R1 by raising InvalidKeyError.
ES512 and the ES521 compatibility alias must reject EC keys not on P-521/SECP521R1 by raising InvalidKeyError.
Curve validation must apply whether the caller passes an EC key object directly or provides PEM- or SSH-encoded EC key material that is parsed during key preparation.
ECAlgorithm instances created without an expected curve must continue to accept supported EC keys without curve-specific rejection.
acceptance_criteria: When an application signs or verifies with ES256 and supplies an EC key that is not on P-256/SECP256R1, the operation should fail with InvalidKeyError.
When an application signs or verifies with ES256K and supplies an EC key that is not on secp256k1/SECP256K1, the operation should fail with InvalidKeyError.
When an application signs or verifies with ES384 and supplies an EC key that is not on P-384/SECP384R1, the operation should fail with InvalidKeyError.
When an application signs or verifies with ES512 or ES521 and supplies an EC key that is not on P-521/SECP521R1, the operation should fail with InvalidKeyError.
When an application uses a correctly matched EC key for the selected default ES algorithm, key preparation should accept the key and JWT processing should proceed normally.
When a caller provides a valid EC key as an already loaded key object or as PEM/SSH text, the same curve-matching rule should be enforced for the selected default ES algorithm.
When a caller constructs ECAlgorithm without an expected curve, supported EC curves should continue to be accepted as before.

task_5.title: Enforce string issuer claim validation in JWT encode and decode flows
task_5.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 tightens issuer validation so JWT payloads cannot use a non-string `iss` claim during encoding, and issuer verification during decoding rejects malformed issuer claims or invalid issuer parameter types with library-defined errors instead of allowing ambiguous behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT issuer handling enforces the `iss` claim as a string and that issuer verification during decode fails predictably when the token issuer claim or supplied issuer value is invalid.

expectation.grounded: Calls to `jwt.encode` or `PyJWT.encode` must reject payloads whose `iss` claim is present but not a string by raising `TypeError`. During issuer validation in decode paths, `_validate_iss` must continue to require the `iss` claim when an `issuer` value is supplied, must reject tokens whose `iss` claim is not a string with `InvalidIssuerError`, must accept `issuer` as either a single string or a `Container[str]`, and must raise `InvalidIssuerError` when the provided issuer does not match or when the `issuer` parameter is not a valid string/container input.
expectation.conceptual: JWT issuer values must be treated as textual identifiers. Encoding should fail fast if a token payload uses a non-text issuer, and decoding with issuer verification should only accept tokens whose issuer is a string that matches the expected issuer or one of the allowed issuers. Invalid issuer inputs should produce issuer-related validation errors rather than undefined type-driven failures.

constraints.grounded: If no `issuer` is supplied for issuer validation, this change should not introduce new issuer checks in that path. When an `issuer` is supplied and the payload lacks `iss`, the existing missing-claim behavior must remain intact. Successful validation must still support exact matching for a single issuer string and membership matching against standard container inputs such as lists, tuples, or sets of strings.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should narrow invalid issuer handling without changing unrelated JWT behavior. Existing valid string-based issuer workflows must keep working, missing issuer claims should still be reported through the established required-claim path, and multi-issuer allowlists should remain supported.

behavior: Encoding a JWT with an `iss` claim that is not a string now fails with `TypeError` instead of producing a token.
Issuer verification during decode now rejects tokens whose `iss` claim exists but is not a string by raising `InvalidIssuerError`.
Decode-time issuer matching accepts either a single issuer string or a container of allowed issuer strings.
If an allowed-issuer container is provided and the token issuer is not contained in it, decode raises `InvalidIssuerError`.
If the `issuer` argument supplied for validation is not a string or compatible container value, issuer validation raises `InvalidIssuerError` instead of surfacing a raw type-related failure.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller encodes a payload containing `iss` as a non-string value, the encode operation should fail with `TypeError`.
When a caller decodes a token with issuer verification enabled and the token does not include `iss`, the operation should fail with the existing missing required claim behavior for `iss`.
When a caller decodes a token with issuer verification enabled and the token `iss` value is not a string, the operation should fail with `InvalidIssuerError`.
When a caller decodes a token with `issuer` set to a string, decoding should succeed only if the token `iss` exactly matches that string.
When a caller decodes a token with `issuer` set to a container of strings, decoding should succeed only if the token `iss` matches one of the allowed values.
When a caller passes an invalid non-string, non-container `issuer` value for issuer verification, decoding should fail with `InvalidIssuerError`.

task_3.title: Reject mismatched asymmetric key families during JWT verification
task_3.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 tightens asymmetric key validation for RSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA algorithms so incompatible key material is rejected early and consistently, avoiding low-level cryptography failures during decode, sign, and verify flows.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT operations reject asymmetric keys that do not belong to the selected algorithm family, so using RSA, ECDSA, or EdDSA algorithms with incompatible key material fails as an invalid-key condition instead of surfacing low-level cryptography type errors.

expectation.grounded: When cryptography-backed algorithms are used through `jwt.decode` or directly through `RSAAlgorithm`, `ECAlgorithm`, or `OKPAlgorithm`, key preparation should validate that the supplied key object or parsed PEM/SSH key belongs to the algorithm's allowed key family. Mismatched key families should raise `InvalidKeyError` before sign or verify is attempted. `Algorithm.check_crypto_key_type` should raise `ValueError` when cryptography support is unavailable or when called from a non-cryptography algorithm. If an `ECAlgorithm` instance is configured with an expected curve, it should also reject elliptic-curve keys on a different curve with `InvalidKeyError`.
expectation.conceptual: JWT signing and verification should confirm that the provided asymmetric key matches the selected algorithm type before using it. Incompatible RSA, elliptic-curve, and EdDSA keys should be rejected immediately with a clear invalid-key failure, and any explicit elliptic-curve restriction should be enforced when applicable.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress successful handling of valid RSA, elliptic-curve, or Ed25519/Ed448 public/private keys provided as cryptography key objects, PEM text, PEM bytes, or supported SSH public keys. Preserve invalid-key behavior for unparseable key material, and keep cryptography key-family validation limited to cryptography-based algorithms.
constraints.conceptual: Keys that already match the selected algorithm should continue to work unchanged. The update should only make incompatible or unsupported asymmetric keys fail earlier and more clearly, without changing non-cryptography algorithm behavior.

behavior: Using an RSA algorithm with key material that parses as a non-RSA cryptography key should fail during key preparation with `InvalidKeyError` instead of reaching cryptography verification and surfacing a low-level `TypeError`.
`RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key` should only accept RSA public/private keys, whether supplied directly as cryptography objects or loaded from PEM or supported SSH input.
`ECAlgorithm.prepare_key` should only accept elliptic-curve public/private keys, whether supplied directly as cryptography objects or loaded from PEM or supported SSH input.
`OKPAlgorithm.prepare_key` should only accept Ed25519 or Ed448 public/private keys, whether supplied directly as cryptography objects or loaded from PEM or supported SSH input.
`OKPAlgorithm.prepare_key` should reject string or byte input that is not recognizable as public or private key material with `InvalidKeyError`.

`Algorithm.check_crypto_key_type` should raise `ValueError` if cryptography support is unavailable or if the algorithm does not define cryptography key-family validation, and should raise `InvalidKeyError` for mismatched cryptography key families.
If `ECAlgorithm` is instantiated with an expected curve, supplying an elliptic-curve key on a different curve should raise `InvalidKeyError` before signing or verification proceeds.
acceptance_criteria: When `jwt.decode` or signature verification is performed with an RSA algorithm and the supplied key resolves to an elliptic-curve or EdDSA key, it should fail with `InvalidKeyError` rather than a low-level cryptography `TypeError`.
When RSA, ECDSA, or EdDSA operations are given matching cryptography key objects or supported PEM/SSH encodings for the correct key family, they should continue to prepare the key successfully.
When `ECAlgorithm` receives a parsed or direct key from the wrong cryptographic family, it should reject the key with `InvalidKeyError` before attempting signing or verification.
When `OKPAlgorithm` receives bytes or text that do not identify a supported public or private key, it should reject the input as an invalid key.
When `Algorithm.check_crypto_key_type` is invoked without cryptography support or from a non-cryptography algorithm, it should raise `ValueError`.
When an `ECAlgorithm` instance is configured with a specific curve expectation and a different elliptic-curve key is supplied, it should reject that key with `InvalidKeyError` before use.

task_7.title: Support fractional JWK cache lifespan and timeout values
task_7.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 updates the public typing contract for JWK cache lifespan and client timeout parameters so callers can use floating-point durations, including sub-second timeouts, without type-checking friction while preserving existing integer-based usage.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWK client timeout and cache lifespan parameters are supported as floating-point durations so users can supply fractional values, while keeping existing integer-based usage valid and unchanged.

expectation.grounded: The public constructor signatures for `PyJWKClient` and `JWKSetCache` should treat `timeout` and `lifespan` as `float`-typed duration values. `PyJWKClient.__init__` should accept a `float` for `timeout` and `lifespan`, and `JWKSetCache.__init__` should accept a `float` for `lifespan`, so callers can pass values such as sub-second timeouts without static typing conflicts.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to configure JWK retrieval timeouts and cache lifetimes with fractional durations, and those values should be recognized as part of the supported public API rather than as type mismatches.

constraints.grounded: Existing callers that pass integer values to `PyJWKClient` or `JWKSetCache` must remain valid. This upgrade should not change the meaning of cache configuration, request timeout behavior, or other constructor options beyond broadening the declared duration types to include floating-point values.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must be backward compatible for existing duration settings and should only expand the accepted contract to include fractional values, without introducing unrelated behavior changes.

behavior: `PyJWKClient` exposes `timeout` as a floating-point duration parameter in its public API contract.
`PyJWKClient` exposes `lifespan` as a floating-point cache duration parameter in its public API contract.
`JWKSetCache` exposes `lifespan` as a floating-point cache duration parameter in its public API contract.
Fractional duration inputs, including sub-second timeout values, are treated as supported caller inputs rather than type-level mismatches.
Integer duration inputs remain acceptable and retain their existing behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a user instantiates `PyJWKClient` with a fractional `timeout` value such as `0.5`, the library should treat that argument as a valid supported input.
When a user instantiates `PyJWKClient` with a fractional `lifespan` value, the library should treat that cache duration as a valid supported input.
When a user instantiates `JWKSetCache` with a fractional `lifespan` value, the library should treat that cache duration as a valid supported input.
When existing code passes integer values for `timeout` or `lifespan`, it should continue to work without any contract regression.

When users rely on the public API surface for these duration parameters, the library should present fractional durations as first-class supported values rather than as unsupported or incompatible usage.

task_9.title: Reuse a Shared Wheel to Speed Up Test Setup
task_9.description: Version 2.11.0 introduces a contributor-facing build optimization that reuses a single built wheel across test environments to reduce local and CI setup time. The provided release note and empty code diff do not evidence any public API or runtime behavior change for library consumers.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.11.0 remains behaviorally transparent for application runtime usage while improving contributor and CI workflow efficiency by avoiding redundant package builds during multi-environment test setup.

expectation.grounded: Based on the release note and the absence of runtime code changes in the provided diff, the upgrade should not add, remove, or alter public library runtime behavior. The evidenced change is limited to the project's test/build workflow, where a shared wheel is built once and reused across tox environments to reduce setup time.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should feel the same to applications using the library, with the only intended benefit being faster maintainer and CI setup when running the project's test matrix.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime semantics, warnings, exceptions, configuration requirements, or migration steps for library consumers. Preserve existing observable behavior outside the development and test environment setup workflow.
constraints.conceptual: Keep production usage unchanged. Limit the effect of this update to development-time efficiency improvements rather than behavior changes visible to application users.

behavior: The project's multi-environment test workflow should reuse a single built distribution artifact instead of rebuilding it separately for each tox environment.
Development and CI setup time for running the test suite should be reduced relative to the prior repeated-build workflow.
No new user-visible runtime behavior changes are evidenced for normal library consumption in applications.

When maintainers run multiple tox environments, package build work should be shared rather than repeated independently for each environment.
When the library is used in production rather than in the project's test workflow, it should exhibit the same observable behavior as before this change.

task_6.title: Make Decode Options Typed and Consistent
task_6.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 formalizes the supported option contract for JWT decoding and aligns option merging so decode and decode_complete behave predictably when callers disable signature verification or supply custom decode options. The update also exposes the full option surface, including strict audience and minimum key length settings, as documented public option types.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT decoding exposes a clear, supported options contract and applies decode options consistently across `jwt.decode`, `jwt.decode_complete`, and `PyJWT` instances, especially when `verify_signature` is disabled or custom verification options are supplied.

expectation.grounded: `jwt.decode`, `jwt.decode_complete`, and `PyJWT` should accept the documented `jwt.types.Options` contract, while JWS-level signature operations should use `jwt.types.SigOptions`. Merged decode options should include defaults for `verify_signature`, `require`, `strict_aud`, `verify_aud`, `verify_exp`, `verify_iat`, `verify_iss`, `verify_jti`, `verify_nbf`, `verify_sub`, and `enforce_minimum_key_length`. When `verify_signature` is set to `False`, any unspecified `verify_aud`, `verify_exp`, `verify_iat`, `verify_iss`, `verify_jti`, `verify_nbf`, and `verify_sub` checks should default to `False`, while explicitly provided verification flags remain in effect.
expectation.conceptual: Decoding APIs should have a well-defined options schema that users can rely on. Turning off signature verification should also turn off dependent claim validation by default unless the caller explicitly re-enables a specific check, and custom defaults should merge predictably with per-call options.

constraints.grounded: Keep secure defaults intact when no options are provided: signature verification remains enabled, claim requirements are only enforced through `require`, and `strict_aud` and `enforce_minimum_key_length` default to `False`. Preserve the existing deprecation warning behavior around the legacy `verify` argument and extra keyword arguments.
constraints.conceptual: Default decoding behavior should stay secure and backward compatible. Relaxed validation should only happen when a caller opts into it, and existing warning behavior for deprecated decode arguments should not be removed.

behavior: Public typed option definitions are available for JWT decode options (`Options`, `FullOptions`) and JWS signature options (`SigOptions`).
A `PyJWT` instance now materializes a complete decode option set, including `strict_aud` and `enforce_minimum_key_length`, rather than relying on a partial options dictionary.
When decode options disable `verify_signature`, unspecified claim-verification flags default to disabled so claim validation does not continue implicitly.
Explicit per-claim verification overrides continue to take precedence even when `verify_signature` is disabled globally.
Required-claim enforcement continues to depend on the configured `require` list and should raise the library's missing-required-claim error when a required claim is absent or null.
acceptance_criteria: When `jwt.decode` or `jwt.decode_complete` is called without an `options` argument, it should verify the token signature and apply the normal default claim-validation behavior.

When a caller passes `options` with `verify_signature=False` and does not set individual `verify_*` flags, decoding should skip signature verification and also skip the related `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `iss`, `jti`, `nbf`, and `sub` validations.
When a caller passes `verify_signature=False` together with an explicit `verify_*` override such as `verify_exp=True`, decoding should preserve that explicit claim-validation setting.
When a claim name appears in `require`, decoding should fail with the existing missing-required-claim error if that claim is missing or null.

When users rely on the documented decode option surface, the supported options should include signature verification, required-claim enforcement, strict audience handling, per-claim verification toggles, and minimum key length enforcement with defined defaults.

task_8.title: Remove invalid-escape warnings from JWT decode APIs
task_8.description: The 2.11.0 update removes import-time SyntaxWarning and DeprecationWarning noise caused by invalid escape sequences in JWT decoding API documentation strings, and clarifies the published decode and decode_complete API contract for issuer inputs and returned dictionary shapes without changing normal decoding behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that importing the JWT decoding APIs does not emit invalid-escape SyntaxWarning or DeprecationWarning noise, and ensure that the public decode contract clearly reflects the supported issuer input form and the dictionary-shaped return values of decode-related APIs.

expectation.grounded: Importing the module that defines `PyJWT.decode()` and `PyJWT.decode_complete()` must not emit `SyntaxWarning` or `DeprecationWarning` caused by invalid escape sequences in those APIs' documentation text. The public contract should present `issuer` as `str | Container[str] | None`, `PyJWT.decode()` as returning a claims dictionary, and `PyJWT.decode_complete()` as returning a dictionary with `header`, `payload`, and `signature` entries.
expectation.conceptual: Upgrading users should be able to import and use the JWT decoding APIs without spurious interpreter warnings, and the published API surface should accurately describe what issuer values are accepted and what decoded data is returned.

constraints.grounded: Do not alter the existing token validation flow, deprecated extra-kwargs warning behavior, or the observable data returned by `PyJWT.decode()` and `PyJWT.decode_complete()` beyond making their documented and typed contract accurate. The change should be limited to removing invalid-escape import warnings and preserving current decode semantics.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should be non-breaking for normal JWT decoding. It should eliminate warning noise and improve API clarity without changing how tokens are validated or the structure of successful decode results.

behavior: Importing the module that exposes `PyJWT.decode()` and `PyJWT.decode_complete()` no longer triggers interpreter warnings caused by invalid escape sequences in their algorithm examples.
`PyJWT.decode()` is published as returning a dictionary of JWT claims rather than an unconstrained value.
`PyJWT.decode_complete()` is published as returning a dictionary containing the JOSE header, JWT payload, and JWT signature.
The public typing and documentation for `issuer` accept either a single issuer string or a container of issuer strings for issuer validation.
acceptance_criteria: When an application imports the JWT API module on supported Python versions, it should not receive `SyntaxWarning` or `DeprecationWarning` attributable to invalid escape sequences in the decode API documentation.
When a caller relies on the public contract for `PyJWT.decode()`, it should indicate that the return value is a claims dictionary.
When a caller relies on the public contract for `PyJWT.decode_complete()`, it should indicate that the return value is a dictionary containing `header`, `payload`, and `signature`.
When a caller configures issuer validation with either a single string or a container of issuer strings, the public API contract should represent that usage as supported.

task_12.title: Replace deprecated pep517 build flow
task_12.description: Version 2.11.0 updates the package-building workflow to use the supported `build` package instead of the deprecated `pep517.build` path. The provided release note frames this as a maintenance change to remove deprecation warnings during package build validation, with no evidenced runtime API or behavior change for library consumers.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.11.0 replaces deprecated `pep517`-based package build validation with the supported `build` tooling, while preserving existing runtime library behavior for consumers.

expectation.grounded: The package-building workflow should use the `build` package rather than `pep517.build` when validating or producing distributable artifacts. Based on the provided materials, no public runtime API additions, removals, or behavioral changes are evidenced for application-facing library usage.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should modernize how the package is built so maintainers no longer rely on deprecated build tooling. For application developers, the library should behave the same at runtime after the upgrade.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime requirements, public API changes, or application-code migration needs for existing consumers. Preserve successful package build outcomes while eliminating reliance on the deprecated `pep517.build` entry point.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the change limited to build-tooling maintenance. The upgrade should not alter how developers use the library in their applications.

behavior: Package build validation uses the supported `build` package instead of the deprecated `pep517.build` path.
Build-related deprecation warnings attributable to `pep517.build` are no longer expected during package build workflows.
No user-visible runtime behavior change is evidenced for existing library consumers as part of this upgrade.
acceptance_criteria: When the package build workflow is run after upgrading to 2.11.0, it should invoke supported `build`-based tooling rather than the deprecated `pep517.build` path.
When maintainers build or validate release artifacts under the upgraded workflow, the process should not emit deprecation warnings caused by `pep517.build`.
When an application upgrades from 2.10.1 to 2.11.0, it should not need runtime code changes solely because of this update.

task_11.title: Add official Python 3.14 and PyPy 3.10/3.11 support
task_11.description: The 2.11.0 update expands the library's officially supported Python runtimes to include CPython 3.14 and PyPy 3.10 and 3.11. The provided code diff contains no production changes, so the upgrade is characterized as a compatibility and support-matrix update rather than a runtime behavior change.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the library officially supports CPython 3.14 and PyPy 3.10 and 3.11 while preserving existing user-facing JWT behavior for already supported runtimes.

expectation.grounded: Version 2.11.0 should recognize CPython 3.14, PyPy 3.10, and PyPy 3.11 as supported interpreter targets. Based on the provided materials, no public JWT API, return value, warning, or exception behavior is evidenced to change because the supplied production code diff is empty.
expectation.conceptual: Upgrading should broaden the set of supported Python runtimes without changing how applications interact with the library or how existing JWT workflows behave.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime-facing API changes, behavioral regressions, or compatibility breaks in existing JWT operations as part of this support update. Treat the change as an expansion of interpreter compatibility only unless additional production code evidence exists.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should add platform support, not alter established application behavior.

behavior: The supported runtime matrix now includes CPython 3.14.
The supported runtime matrix now includes PyPy 3.10 and PyPy 3.11.
No production runtime behavior change is evidenced by the provided code diff, so existing public library behavior should remain unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When the package's supported platforms are evaluated, it should include CPython 3.14.
When the package's supported platforms are evaluated, it should include PyPy 3.10 and PyPy 3.11.
When an application upgrades from 2.10.1 to 2.11.0 and uses existing public JWT functionality on previously supported runtimes, it should not observe new behavior changes attributable to this update.

task_10.title: Refine PyJWT public typing contracts for supported Python versions
task_10.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 tightens and completes public type annotations across the library, with Python 3.9-compatible aliasing and clearer API contracts for algorithms, JWT options, JWK helpers, and decoded object shapes, while preserving existing signing, verification, and decode behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.11.0 provides complete, Python-version-compatible public typing for PyJWT APIs, including key, token, option, and JWK-related interfaces, without changing normal JWT signing, verification, serialization, or decode behavior.

expectation.grounded: Expose fully annotated public contracts for `jwt.algorithms`, `PyJWT`, `PyJWS`, `PyJWKClient`, and `jwt.help.info`. Keep `Algorithm.to_jwk` and concrete HMAC, RSA, EC, and OKP `to_jwk` overloads typed by input key family and by `as_dict` return shape. Define cryptography-backed key aliases in a way that remains valid on supported Python versions, including Python 3.9 compatibility. Treat `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` as accepting `str` or `bytes` token input and returning a `PyJWK`. Represent decoded JWT payloads and JWS headers as JSON object dictionaries, and keep `PyJWT` option handling typed as structured option sets.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should make the library's public typing accurate and complete for supported Python versions so that IDEs, static analyzers, and generated documentation correctly describe supported key types, token inputs, options, and decoded JWT/JWS object shapes, while the runtime behavior users already depend on stays the same.

constraints.grounded: Do not change which runtime key families are accepted for HMAC, RSA, EC, and OKP algorithms. Do not change `to_jwk` behavior: `as_dict=True` must still produce a JWK dictionary and the default path must still produce a serialized JWK string. Keep signing methods returning `bytes`, preserve existing verification semantics, and preserve decode failures for invalid JSON header or payload content and for payloads that are not JSON objects. `cryptography` must remain optional for cryptography-backed typing aliases.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade is a typing-contract refinement, not a cryptographic or serialization behavior change. Existing JWT encode/decode flows, JWK serialization modes, supported key categories, and current error conditions must remain stable.

behavior: `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` recognizes both text and byte JWT inputs as part of its public API contract and returns the matching `PyJWK` signing key.
`Algorithm.to_jwk` and the HMAC, RSA, EC, and OKP `to_jwk` variants preserve their dual return contract: a JWK object mapping when `as_dict=True`, otherwise a serialized JWK string.
`PyJWT` exposes typed option shapes for full JWT options and signature-related options, and its per-instance JWS helper is initialized from the signature option subset.
Decoded JWS headers and JWT payloads are treated as JSON object dictionaries; invalid JSON still raises `DecodeError`, and payloads that decode to non-object JSON remain rejected.

Public key type aliases for RSA, EC, and OKP algorithms are available in a Python 3.9-compatible form for type checking and documentation generation, including fallback support where `TypeAlias` is not provided by the standard library.
acceptance_criteria: When a consumer type-checks code using PyJWT on Python 3.9, the published annotations should remain valid without relying on Python 3.10 union-syntax-only features.

When a caller uses `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` with either a `str` JWT or a `bytes` JWT representing the same token, the API contract should treat both inputs as supported and return the same matching signing key.
When a caller invokes any public `to_jwk` overload with `as_dict=True`, it should expose a JWK mapping result; when `as_dict` is omitted or false, it should expose a serialized JWK string result.
When JWT payload JSON or JWS header JSON is malformed, decoding should continue to fail with `DecodeError` rather than changing to a different failure mode.
When a decoded payload is valid JSON but not a JSON object, it should still be rejected rather than being treated as a valid JWT payload.

task_16.title: Document leeway support for nbf validation
task_16.description: The 2.11.0 update clarifies that JWT decode-time leeway applies not only to expiration-related validation but also to the not-before (`nbf`) claim. This is a documentation-focused release item intended to help users account for clock skew when validating tokens that may become valid slightly before or after the local system time.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that users understand that configuring decode-time leeway also affects validation of the `nbf` claim, so JWTs can tolerate expected clock skew around their not-before time.

expectation.grounded: PyJWT's documented decode behavior should explicitly state that the existing `leeway` option applies during `nbf` claim validation. When a token's `nbf` time is slightly in the future relative to the validator's clock, the configured leeway window should be taken into account before the token is treated as not yet valid.
expectation.conceptual: Token validation should clearly support a clock-skew tolerance window for not-before checks, not just other time-based claims. Users should be able to rely on one leeway setting to avoid rejecting tokens that are only marginally early because of timing differences between systems.

constraints.grounded: This upgrade item should not introduce a new public API or alter unrelated claim-validation rules; it documents that the existing `leeway` mechanism covers `nbf` validation as part of decode-time verification.
constraints.conceptual: The change should remain a clarification of existing behavior rather than a broader redesign of JWT validation. Other validation expectations should stay the same unless already governed by the existing leeway behavior.

behavior: Decode-time leeway is part of the validation semantics for the `nbf` claim.
A JWT with an `nbf` timestamp slightly ahead of the validator's current time should still be considered valid when the difference falls within the configured leeway window.
If the `nbf` timestamp exceeds the allowed leeway window, the token should continue to be treated as not yet valid.
acceptance_criteria: When an application decodes a JWT and provides a leeway value, the documented behavior should state that the same leeway is used for `nbf` validation.
When a token's `nbf` is only slightly in the future and that gap is no greater than the configured leeway, the token should be accepted as valid.
When a token's `nbf` is further in the future than the configured leeway allows, the token should still be rejected as not yet valid.
When no leeway is configured, `nbf` validation should continue to use the normal strict time comparison.

task_18.title: Document JWT sub and jti registered claims
task_18.description: The 2.11.0 update completes the JWT registered-claims documentation by explicitly covering the `sub` and `jti` claims, including the role of `jti` in replay-attack prevention. Based on the provided artifacts, this is a documentation-only change with no runtime behavior change from 2.10.1.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the library documentation fully describes the registered JWT claims by explicitly documenting the `sub` and `jti` claims, clarifying their intended purpose and preserving existing runtime behavior.

expectation.grounded: Public documentation for JWT claim handling should list `sub` as a registered claim name and document `jti` as a registered claim used for token identification and replay-attack prevention. Since the provided code diff contains no runtime changes, existing encode/decode behavior for tokens containing these claims should remain unchanged in 2.11.0.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.11.0 should find complete guidance for the standard JWT claims, including what `sub` and `jti` represent, without experiencing any behavioral change in how tokens are processed.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new validation rules, exceptions, warnings, or claim-processing semantics for `sub` or `jti` based on this update alone. The change is limited to documentation completeness according to the provided release note and empty code diff.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should improve clarity only. Applications that already issue or consume tokens with `sub` or `jti` should continue to behave the same way after upgrading.

behavior: The documented set of registered JWT claims now explicitly includes `sub`.
The documented set of registered JWT claims now explicitly includes `jti`.
Documentation now explains that `jti` can be used to help prevent replay attacks.
No runtime behavior change is evidenced for token encoding, decoding, validation, or error handling in this update.
acceptance_criteria: When a user reads the JWT registered-claims documentation in 2.11.0, it should explicitly describe the `sub` claim.
When a user reads the JWT registered-claims documentation in 2.11.0, it should explicitly describe the `jti` claim.
When a user consults the documentation for `jti`, it should explain its purpose in identifying tokens and supporting replay-attack prevention.
When upgrading from 2.10.1 to 2.11.0, applications using `sub` or `jti` claims should observe no change in runtime processing behavior attributable to this update.

task_19.title: Modernize type annotations without changing runtime behavior
task_19.description: The 2.11.0 update introduces typing modernization driven by pyupgrade-related cleanup. Deprecated `typing` collection aliases are replaced by their modern equivalents, and generic annotations use built-in collection types where applicable. This is an internal/type-surface cleanup and does not introduce a user-visible runtime feature or behavioral change.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.11.0 preserves existing runtime behavior while reflecting the library's modernized typing surface, including replacement of deprecated `typing` collection aliases and use of standard built-in generic annotations where applicable.

expectation.grounded: The upgraded library should remain behaviorally equivalent at runtime to 2.10.1 while adopting modern Python typing forms. References that previously relied on deprecated aliases such as `typing.X` for collection interfaces should be represented with the corresponding modern collection abstractions, and collection generics should use built-in forms such as `dict` and `list` instead of legacy `Dict` and `List` aliases where those annotations are exposed.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, the library should behave the same for application code, but its type information should align with modern Python typing conventions. Consumers should not need to change runtime usage, and any type-aware tooling should see a cleaner, up-to-date annotation style rather than deprecated collection aliases.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime APIs, warnings, exceptions, or behavior changes as part of this update. Existing public runtime semantics must remain unchanged; the change is limited to typing-style modernization indicated by the release note.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade must be non-disruptive for existing users. It should not change how the library is imported, called, or behaves in production; only the typing representation should be modernized.

behavior: The upgrade does not add a new runtime feature or fix a user-visible runtime defect.
Type annotations are modernized to avoid deprecated `typing` collection aliases in favor of current collection abstractions.
Collection generic annotations use standard built-in generic forms instead of older `typing` container aliases where applicable.
Observable runtime behavior, including imports and normal library usage, remains unchanged relative to 2.10.1.
acceptance_criteria: When upgrading from 2.10.1 to 2.11.0, existing application code should continue to run without any runtime behavior change attributable to this update.
When users interact with the library through its normal public runtime API, it should not emit new warnings, raise new exceptions, or require code changes because of this release.
When users or tools inspect the library's exposed type information, deprecated `typing` collection aliases should no longer be the expected annotation style.
When collection generics are represented in the library's type surface, they should follow modern built-in generic notation rather than legacy `typing` container aliases.

task_15.title: Stabilize PyJWT key typing and documentation builds
task_15.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 makes its documented key-type aliases available during Sphinx-based API documentation builds and tightens the typed JWT/JWS option surface so `PyJWT` consistently owns and forwards signature-related configuration to its internal JWS handling.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.11.0 preserves a usable public key-type and option surface for API documentation builds, while keeping `PyJWT` encode/decode behavior consistent when JWT options are merged and delegated to internal JWS processing.

expectation.grounded: During Sphinx builds signaled by `SPHINX_BUILD`, the public `jwt.algorithms` aliases `AllowedPrivateKeys` and `AllowedPublicKeys` must remain available for autodoc even when they would otherwise only exist for type checking. In `jwt.api_jwt`, `PyJWT` should expose typed key inputs via `AllowedPrivateKeyTypes` and `AllowedPublicKeyTypes`, accept `PyJWK`, `str`, and `bytes` regardless of cryptography availability, use merged `Options`/`FullOptions` state, and construct an internal `PyJWS` using the signature-related subset of those options. Decode APIs should also accept `issuer` values typed as `Container[str]` rather than only sequence-like collections.
expectation.conceptual: The library should keep its documented key aliases visible to documentation tooling, and JWT operations should continue to accept the documented key forms while applying JWT and JWS options consistently through a single configured object model.

constraints.grounded: Do not make the optional cryptography dependency a prerequisite for documentation builds that only need public aliases rendered. When cryptography is unavailable, keep the usable public key input surface limited to `PyJWK`, text keys, and byte keys. Preserve default verification behavior unless callers explicitly override options, and keep decode/decode_complete compatible with container-style issuer collections.
constraints.conceptual: Documentation-only environments should not fail because optional crypto types are missing, and existing token verification defaults should remain stable apart from the clarified accepted input shapes and internal option propagation.

behavior: `jwt.algorithms` now materializes its documented key aliases during Sphinx builds so autodoc can resolve `AllowedPrivateKeys` and `AllowedPublicKeys` without missing-member failures.
`jwt.api_jwt` defines composite key input types for `PyJWT` that include `PyJWK`, `str`, and `bytes`, and include cryptography-backed key objects when cryptography is installed.
`PyJWT` now initializes and owns an internal `PyJWS` instance instead of depending only on module-level JWS helpers.
`PyJWT` derives and forwards signature-related options from its merged JWT option set into the internal `PyJWS` configuration.
Decode and decode-complete issuer inputs are widened from sequence-oriented typing to container-oriented typing, allowing membership-based issuer collections.
acceptance_criteria: When API docs are built with `SPHINX_BUILD` enabled, autodoc should be able to resolve the documented `jwt.algorithms` key aliases without missing-attribute warnings caused solely by type-checking-only definitions.

When an application uses `PyJWT.encode`, `PyJWT.decode`, or `PyJWT.decode_complete`, it should accept `PyJWK`, string keys, and byte keys as documented inputs, and also accept supported cryptography key objects when cryptography is installed.
When a `PyJWT` instance is created with custom options, the signature-related portion of those options should be reflected in the internal JWS behavior used by JWT operations.
When callers rely on default verification settings, upgrading should preserve the default verified-decode behavior unless options explicitly disable parts of verification.
When callers pass an issuer allow-list or other container-like issuer collection to decode APIs, the value should be accepted as a valid issuer input shape.

task_20.title: Add configurable minimum key length validation for HMAC and RSA JWT operations
task_20.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 adds security validation for undersized HMAC secrets and RSA keys during JWT signing and signature verification. Short keys now emit a dedicated warning by default for backward compatibility, and callers can opt into strict enforcement so the same condition fails with an invalid-key error.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT signing and signature verification detect insecure HMAC and RSA key sizes, warn by default for backward compatibility, and support opt-in strict rejection of undersized keys.

expectation.grounded: When using PyJWT or PyJWS with HMAC or RSA algorithms, signature operations should evaluate key length after key preparation. HMAC keys shorter than the selected hash digest size and RSA keys smaller than 2048 bits should emit jwt.InsecureKeyLengthWarning by default. When options include enforce_minimum_key_length=True, the same condition should raise jwt.exceptions.InvalidKeyError instead. This behavior should apply to both token creation and signature verification, and the warning type should be available as jwt.InsecureKeyLengthWarning.
expectation.conceptual: JWT operations should surface insecure signing material to callers. By default, existing flows should remain compatible but emit a dedicated warning when an HMAC secret or RSA key is below the library's minimum recommendation. Applications that require strict enforcement should be able to opt in so the operation fails with an invalid-key error rather than proceeding.

constraints.grounded: Do not change behavior for algorithms that do not define a minimum key length check. Keep strict enforcement disabled by default for compatibility. The minimum thresholds must remain algorithm-specific: HMAC uses the digest output size of the selected HS* algorithm, and RSA uses 2048 bits. The warning-versus-error policy must be consistent between signing and verification paths.
constraints.conceptual: Only undersized HMAC and RSA keys should be affected. Existing callers should not be forced into failures unless they explicitly enable strict enforcement, and keys that satisfy the minimum recommendation should continue to work without new warnings or errors.

behavior: Signing or encoding with an HMAC key shorter than the digest length for the selected HS* algorithm emits InsecureKeyLengthWarning by default.
Signing or encoding with an RSA key smaller than 2048 bits emits InsecureKeyLengthWarning by default.
Verifying a JWT signature with an undersized HMAC or RSA key emits the same warning by default.
Supplying enforce_minimum_key_length=True in PyJWT or PyJWS options turns those warnings into InvalidKeyError failures.
HMAC and RSA keys that meet the minimum recommendations continue through normal signing and verification without this key-length warning or error.
The dedicated warning type is exported as jwt.InsecureKeyLengthWarning so callers can observe or filter it.
acceptance_criteria: When an application signs a token with HS256 using a secret shorter than 32 bytes and strict enforcement is disabled, it should still produce the token and emit InsecureKeyLengthWarning.

When an application verifies a token with HS384 or HS512 using a secret shorter than the corresponding digest length and strict enforcement is disabled, it should emit InsecureKeyLengthWarning during verification.
When an application signs or verifies with an RSA key smaller than 2048 bits and strict enforcement is disabled, it should emit InsecureKeyLengthWarning and continue the cryptographic operation.
When enforce_minimum_key_length=True is supplied through PyJWT or PyJWS options, any HMAC or RSA key below the minimum recommendation should cause InvalidKeyError instead of a warning.
When an HMAC or RSA key meets the minimum recommendation, signing and verification should behave as before without InsecureKeyLengthWarning or InvalidKeyError related to key length.
When a non-HMAC and non-RSA algorithm is used, this feature should not introduce new minimum-key-length warnings or errors.

task_21.title: Isolate PyJWT JWS state and tighten issuer validation
task_21.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 refactors `PyJWT` to use instance-owned JWS state so signing and verification options are applied consistently per handler, and it tightens issuer claim validation during token creation and issuer-based decoding.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.11.0 preserves expected JWT encode and decode usage while making `PyJWT` instance options apply consistently to signing and verification, and ensure issuer claims are validated strictly as strings during both token creation and issuer matching.

expectation.grounded: A `jwt.api_jwt.PyJWT` instance should own and use its own `PyJWS` state instead of routing `encode()`, `decode()`, and `decode_complete()` through module-level `api_jws` helpers. Constructor options and per-call options should be merged consistently, with JWS-level options such as `verify_signature` and `enforce_minimum_key_length` honored by operations performed through that `PyJWT` instance. When `verify_signature` is disabled, the related claim-verification flags (`verify_exp`, `verify_nbf`, `verify_iat`, `verify_aud`, `verify_iss`, `verify_sub`, `verify_jti`) should default to disabled unless explicitly enabled. `encode()` should raise `TypeError` if the payload `iss` claim is present and not a string. Issuer validation during decode should require the payload `iss` value to be a string, accept either a single issuer string or a `Container[str]` of allowed issuers, and raise `InvalidIssuerError` when the token issuer is invalid or the `issuer` argument is not a valid string-or-container form.
expectation.conceptual: Each JWT handler should behave as if it owns its own signing and verification configuration, so instance-level options work predictably and do not depend on shared global state. Token creation should only accept string issuer claims, and issuer-constrained decoding should only succeed when the token issuer is a valid string that matches the configured allowed issuer or issuer set.

constraints.grounded: Module-level `jwt.encode`, `jwt.decode`, and `jwt.decode_complete` should remain available and continue to behave as the shared global `PyJWT` entry points. Per-call options should still override constructor defaults. If issuer validation is requested and the token omits `iss`, decoding should continue to raise `MissingRequiredClaimError`. Existing audience, subject, expiration, issued-at, not-before, and JWT ID validations should remain governed by their current verification flags and public exception types.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should improve option isolation and issuer validation without removing the existing top-level JWT API or changing unrelated claim-validation rules. Runtime behavior should remain backward-compatible except where stricter issuer type handling and correctly applied instance options are now enforced.

behavior: `PyJWT(options=...)` now applies signature-related configuration through an instance-owned signer/verifier rather than bypassing those settings through global JWS helpers.
Disabling `verify_signature` causes claim-verification flags to default to disabled after options are merged, whether that setting comes from constructor options or per-call options.
`encode()` raises `TypeError` when the payload includes an `iss` claim whose value is not a string.
Decode-time issuer validation raises `InvalidIssuerError` when the token contains an `iss` claim that is present but not a string.

Decode-time issuer matching accepts either a single issuer string or any container of strings used for membership checks, and raises `InvalidIssuerError` when the supplied `issuer` argument is not a valid string or string-container form.
JWS-specific options such as minimum key-length enforcement can be configured on a `PyJWT` instance and are honored by signing and verification operations performed through that instance.
acceptance_criteria: When a `PyJWT` instance is created with signature-related options and `encode()` or `decode_complete()` is called without overriding them, it should honor those instance options rather than behaving as if only module-level defaults exist.

When `verify_signature` is disabled through instance or per-call options, decoding should skip signature verification and should not perform the other claim validations by default unless those claim checks are explicitly enabled.
When `encode()` is called with a payload whose `iss` claim is not a string, it should fail with `TypeError`.

When decoding with an `issuer` constraint and the token omits `iss`, it should raise `MissingRequiredClaimError`; when the token includes `iss` but that claim is not a string, it should raise `InvalidIssuerError`.

When decoding with an `issuer` constraint supplied as a string container, it should accept a token whose string `iss` value is contained in that collection and reject tokens whose issuer is absent from it or whose `issuer` argument is not a valid string-or-container form.

task_17.title: Normalize PyJWT decode options and expose typed option contracts
task_17.description: PyJWT 2.11.0 formalizes the public options surface for JWT decode/signature operations and aligns option-merging behavior so instance-level and per-call configuration are described consistently. The update is primarily about `options` typing and documentation, but it also changes how effective decode options are normalized when signature verification is disabled.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.11.0 provides a consistent, documented `options` contract for `jwt.decode()`, `jwt.decode_complete()`, and `PyJWT(options=...)`, especially when signature verification is disabled and when applications rely on static typing for JWT options and key aliases.

expectation.grounded: PyJWT should expose `jwt.types.Options`, `jwt.types.SigOptions`, and `jwt.types.FullOptions` as the public option shapes for `jwt.decode()`, `jwt.decode_complete()`, `PyJWT`, and `PyJWS`. `PyJWT` should compute its effective options from a complete default set that includes `verify_signature`, `verify_exp`, `verify_nbf`, `verify_iat`, `verify_aud`, `verify_iss`, `verify_sub`, `verify_jti`, `require`, `strict_aud`, and `enforce_minimum_key_length`. When effective options set `verify_signature` to `False`, any unspecified claim-verification flags for exp, nbf, iat, aud, iss, sub, and jti should default to `False`. Signature-related options should be separated into `SigOptions` and passed through to the internal `PyJWS` layer. The documented public surface should also include the `jwt.algorithms` key aliases used by encode/decode signatures.
expectation.conceptual: The library should present one clear, supported configuration model for JWT decoding and signature handling. Callers should be able to understand which options exist, type-check them reliably, and expect disabled signature verification to turn off related claim validation unless those checks are explicitly turned back on.

constraints.grounded: Preserve the existing public decode/decode_complete return shapes, existing warning/deprecation behavior for unsupported extra kwargs and the legacy `verify` argument, and the current validation exception types when the corresponding verification flags remain enabled. Do not require callers to change token formats, algorithm lists, or move away from existing `jwt.decode()` / `jwt.decode_complete()` entry points.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should refine configuration behavior and documentation without changing the basic JWT API shape. Existing successful decode flows should continue to work unless they depended on ambiguous or inconsistent option handling.

behavior: `jwt.decode()` and `jwt.decode_complete()` now have a named public options contract instead of an untyped generic dictionary shape.
`PyJWT(options=...)` now builds its effective configuration from a full default option set and merges caller-supplied options through dedicated option-normalization logic.

If `verify_signature` is disabled in the effective options, unspecified `verify_exp`, `verify_nbf`, `verify_iat`, `verify_aud`, `verify_iss`, `verify_sub`, and `verify_jti` default to disabled rather than implicitly remaining enabled.
Signature-layer configuration is separated into `jwt.types.SigOptions` and initialized on the internal `PyJWS` helper rather than remaining only part of the claim-validation option map.
`strict_aud` and `enforce_minimum_key_length` are part of the supported public option surface for decode/signature configuration.
The public typing/documentation surface now explicitly covers the `PyJWS` APIs and the `jwt.algorithms` key aliases used by encode/decode signatures.
The `issuer` parameter for `decode()` and `decode_complete()` is widened from sequence-only typing to general container typing without changing the issuer-matching contract.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller inspects or type-checks the supported options for `jwt.decode()` or `jwt.decode_complete()`, the library should expose named public option types that cover signature verification, claim verification flags, required claims, strict audience handling, and minimum-key-length enforcement.

When a `PyJWT` instance is created with constructor options, later decode operations should use those options as a normalized base configuration rather than treating constructor options as an ad hoc unstructured mapping.
When effective options have `verify_signature=False` and a specific `verify_*` claim flag is not supplied, validation for exp, nbf, iat, aud, iss, sub, and jti should not run.

When a caller explicitly enables an individual claim check while using the shared options model, that validation should continue to behave as before and raise the same public exception types on failure.
When codebases use static typing against PyJWT, the options and key alias APIs involved in encode/decode flows should resolve as public typed contracts rather than partially unknown mappings.
